lesson.title: The Critical Point: When Liquid and Gas Become Indistinguishable
lesson.summary: Above a substance's critical temperature and critical pressure, the liquid and gas phases become identical in density and merge into a single supercritical fluid that no amount of pressure can condense back into a separate liquid.
lesson.body:
Follow the liquid-gas boundary on a phase diagram, the same kind of map introduced for the triple point, up and to the right, toward higher temperature and pressure, and something strange happens. Raising the temperature makes the liquid expand and its vapor pressure rise; raising the pressure squeezes the gas phase into a smaller volume, increasing its density. Push both far enough and the liquid and the gas start to converge on each other: the liquid gets less dense, the gas gets more dense, until at one specific temperature and pressure, the critical point, their densities become identical and the boundary between them vanishes.

Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure, however large, will condense a gas into a liquid. The molecules simply have too much kinetic energy for intermolecular attractions to hold them into a distinct liquid phase, no matter how tightly they are packed. The critical pressure is the pressure needed to liquefy the substance right at that critical temperature, the last point where a liquid-gas boundary can exist at all.

Push past both the critical temperature and critical pressure simultaneously and the substance becomes a supercritical fluid, a single phase that shares properties with both liquid and gas. It has a density close to a liquid's, meaning it can dissolve materials the way a liquid does, but it also flows and diffuses with the low viscosity of a gas, letting it penetrate porous solids that a true liquid could never soak into. There is no surface tension and no meniscus, because there is no longer a boundary to draw one across.

Water's critical point sits at 374°C (647 K) and about 22.1 MPa. Converting that pressure to atmospheres gives a sense of scale: 22.1 MPa divided by 0.101325 MPa per atmosphere is about 218 atm, over two hundred times normal atmospheric pressure. Carbon dioxide is far gentler to reach: its critical point is only about 31.0°C and roughly 72.8 atm (7.38 MPa), which is why supercritical CO2, not supercritical water, is the workhorse of industrial extraction. It is used to pull caffeine out of coffee beans and extract essential oils without leaving behind the toxic residues a nonpolar organic solvent would.
